# Babysit PR
Your job is to get this PR to a merge-ready state.

Check PR status, comments, and latest CI and resolve any issues until the PR is ready to merge.

1. Merge conflicts: Intelligently resolve any merge conflicts, preserving the intent and correctness of changes on your branch and the base branch. If intents conflict, abort the merge and ask for clarification.
2. Comments: Review active unresolved comments (including Bugbot) and resolve change requests / bug reports where valid. When fetching GitHub comments, filter out resolved threads first. Read only each comment body and the minimum location/URL needed to act on it; do not read the entire JSON output or other unnecessary payload data. Carefully validate issues reported by Bugbot and only take action on those that are valid; explain when you disagree or are unsure.
3. CI: Fix CI issues caused by changes within this PR's scope. Never change CI checks/workflows just to make failures pass, or make unrelated code changes; if that would be required, report back instead. For merge-blocking failures that seem unrelated to this PR, check whether the branch is behind the base branch and merge latest changes, since another PR may have fixed them. Push scoped fixes and re-watch CI until mergeable + green + comments triaged.

--- PRRT_kwDONA5Mxc6dxfg8  | trangdoan982 | apps/roam/src/components/settings/utils/settingsTabs.ts 20
Nine legacy tab ids, one per tab that existed before the taxonomy. Deep links that users saved, plus the three in-repo call sites, resolve through here.

Both "Home" tabs collapse onto Preferences > General because that is where most of their rows landed. Both left sidebar tabs collapse onto the single merged tab.

No unit test covers this map. A wrong entry fails silently by dropping the user on the default tab, so it is worth reading against the tab list in `Settings.tsx`.
--- PRRT_kwDONA5Mxc6dxfjI  | trangdoan982 | apps/roam/src/components/settings/Settings.tsx 172
This was `selectedTabId={visibleTabId}`. The `visibleTabId` guard existed only to bounce the selection off the two `hidden={!leftSidebarEnabled}` left sidebar tabs when the feature was off.

Those two tabs are now one tab that is never hidden, because it hosts the toggle that enables the feature. Nothing can strand the selection, so the guard has no remaining case to protect.
  >> mdroidian : This is a feature we should keep (hiding feature tabs that are disabled).
--- PRRT_kwDONA5Mxc6dxfky  | trangdoan982 | apps/roam/src/components/settings/LeftSidebarSettings.tsx 32
This toggle used to live on Global > Home, one tab away from the settings it controls, because this tab hid itself when the feature was off.

Moving it here means the tab can no longer be feature-gated: a tab that hides itself cannot host the control that un-hides it. The sections it gates are still gated, so no setting becomes reachable that was not before.
  >> mdroidian : One of the benefits we are losing would be hiding the `Left Sidebar` tab when disabled.
Also, this is likely very poor UX for non admin users, who go to the tab and see a blank screen when disabled. (as the "Enable left sidebar" should/will be admin gated).

I believe we should adhere to the original scoping, but I'm not sure if we re-clarified where "feature flags" should live.
--- PRRT_kwDONA5Mxc6dxfmE  | trangdoan982 | apps/roam/src/components/settings/utils/settingAnchor.ts 4
Out of scope for ENG-2189, in service of ENG-2184 (settings search). Called out here so it is not reviewed against this ticket.

The decision worth checking is the addressing scheme: a row is addressed by its setting key path, never as `<tab>/<field>`. A tab-derived address would be invalidated by this very PR, and by every future relocation. Setting key paths already exist in `settingKeys.ts` and do not change when a setting moves tabs.

Nothing reads the attribute yet.
--- PRRT_kwDONA5Mxc6dxgAP  | trangdoan982 | apps/roam/src/components/settings/GeneralSettings.tsx 20
Deleted. Its three rows moved to their taxonomy homes:

- `trigger` to `PreferencesGeneral.tsx`, as the graph-wide half of the Node trigger group
- `Canvas Page Format` to `CanvasSettings.tsx`
- `Enable left sidebar` to `LeftSidebarSettings.tsx`

The `useMemo` resolving the three legacy block uids became `utils/useLegacyConfigUids.ts`, because all three panels still need it and they no longer share a file.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reuse Roam-native colors for section headings**

These custom properties are not defined elsewhere in the repository, so the hard-coded fallback text and border colors always apply. **<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Show the graph-wide trigger in the empty override**

When no personal trigger is configured, explicitly passing an empty placeholder makes the override field completely blank, so it does not show the effective graph-wide trigger and gives no indication of the inherited value. Pass `globalSettings[GLOBAL_KEYS.trigger]` as the placeholder so clearing the override exposes the trigger that will actually be used.

content.text:
CI is green and the PR is still `MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN`. Here's where it stands.

## Fixed and pushed (commit `ENG-2189 Address bot review findings…`)

**Bots**
- **CodeRabbit** — `canvasNodeShortcuts` had no `data-setting-id`. Added `settingAnchor([PERSONAL_KEYS.canvasNodeShortcuts])` on the grid wrapper. Valid, resolved.
- **Codex P1 (CSS)** — valid: `--dg-neutral-dark` / `--dg-border` are defined nowhere in the repo, so only the fallback hexes ever painted. Heading now uses the Blueprint palette with a `.bp3-dark` override, matching the pattern already in [styles.css](apps/roam/src/styles/styles.css:193). Left the thread open since Michael tagged you on it.
- **Codex P2 (trigger placeholder)** — declined the suggested fix: the personal override is an `IKeyCombo`, the graph-wide `trigger` is a trigger character, so showing one as the other's placeholder would mislead. But the blankness it spotted was real, so I reverted the `placeholder=""` and the `placeholder` prop that existed only to pass it — the field shows "Click to set trigger" again, as before this PR. Resolved with that explanation.

**Michael — the ones with an obvious code action** (replied, left unresolved for him)
- `resolveSettingsTabId` — moved the default into the parameter as he asked; `id` is undefined when the plain "Open settings" command opens the dialog with no target tab.
- `useLegacyConfigBlocks` stale-default comment — he's right. ENG-2173 is on `main` but not in this stack's base, so the comment named a default that no longer holds. Reworded to not name one.
- The terse `LegacyConfigBlock` comment ("?") — reworded to say it mirrors the block-sync props the BlockPropSettingPanels take.

Roam typecheck, lint (no new warnings on changed lines), and 142 unit tests pass. The dark-mode heading was not visually verified in a live Roam — it's a color swap plus a new `.bp3-dark` rule, and light-mode behaviour is unchanged.

## Needs you — these are yours to answer

1. **Feature-gated tab hiding** ([Settings.tsx:172](apps/roam/src/components/settings/Settings.tsx:172) + [LeftSidebarSettings.tsx:32](apps/roam/src/components/settings/LeftSidebarSettings.tsx:32)). Michael wants the hide-when-disabled behaviour kept, and flags that a non-admin hitting a blank tab is poor UX once "Enable left sidebar" is admin-gated. He also says he's unsure whether you two re-clarified where feature flags should live. This is the one real design conflict — the tab can't both host the enabling toggle and hide itself, so it needs a decision (move the flag back out to a preferences tab, or accept the always-visible tab).

2. **"Why are we not using tailwind?"** (settingsStyles.css 24 and 34, plus "Roam ships no Tailwind preflight?" on 23). Partly answered in code — the group wrapper is now plain `flex flex-col gap-1` and the dead `dg-settings-group__rows` class is gone. The heading rule stays hand-rolled because `border-b-2` sets only a width; without preflight there's no `border-style`/color default, so it paints nothing. Worth confirming he's happy with that split before I reply on his behalf.

3. **`grid-cols-[auto_auto]` in Roam.** Pre-existing — it came in with #952, not this PR. Roam ships its own compiled Tailwind, so an arbitrary-value class is almost certainly absent and the grid is falling back to a single implicit column. Your call whether to fix it here (out of scope) or file it.

4. **"Can you give an example of a saved deep link?"** ([settingsTabs.ts:19](apps/roam/src/components/settings/utils/settingsTabs.ts:19)) — his skepticism is justified. Nothing parses a tab id out of a URL; the only callers are three in-repo ones, all already updated. So the alias map protects external/stored callers of the exported dialog, not user-saved links. Either the comment should be reworded or the map dropped — I didn't want to delete it unilaterally.

5. **"Can you give an example of this?"** on the `blockKey` comment ([BlockPropSettingPanels.tsx:38](apps/roam/src/components/settings/components/BlockPropSettingPanels.tsx:38)) — concrete answer available: `Canvas Page Format` and `(BETA) Left Sidebar` in `useLegacyConfigBlocks`, whose titles in the UI differ from the block text `discourseConfigRef` matches on. Say the word and I'll post it.

6. FYI only, no action: he noted the discourse context overlay is being removed in ENG-2096.

1. yes, keep the feature-gated tab hiding. explain to me what are the options here first
2. try out tailwind first. confirm whether that works or not. then if it doesn't find out why exactly
3. idk what this is referring to. link. me to the exact comment and explain the feedback here
4. yeah what is "saved deep link"? what is saving it? 
5. hmm i need more explaination for this. i see michael's point: if we only navigate from the setting page ourselves, then we should know when the id is there. there's no entry point where we unilaterally pass in an unknown id

content.text:
Answers to each, in order.

## 2. Tailwind — tested, and it works (already pushed)

Roam serves `assets/css/tailwind.min.css`, a **pre-JIT Tailwind 2 build (~6550 rules)**. I loaded it in the browser and read computed styles off real elements. Three facts:

| class | computed | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `font-semibold` | `600` | works |
| `text-base` / `text-lg` | `14px` / `15.75px` | works, but Roam's root font-size is **14px**, so `1rem ≠ 16px` |
| `border-b-2` | **`0px none`** | paints nothing |
| `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` | `none` | **doesn't exist** |

My original comment was right in substance but named the wrong mechanism, which is why it read as hand-waving. The real reason: `border-b-2` sets *only* `border-bottom-width`. Tailwind's preflight normally supplies `border-style: solid; border-width: 0` for every element — Roam doesn't ship preflight, so with no border-style the browser computes the used width as 0. The fix is `border-0 border-b-2 border-solid`. (Plain `border-solid` without `border-0` is a trap: every other side then inherits the browser's `medium` = 3px.)

So the heading is now Tailwind, and the CSS file holds only what Tailwind can't express — the two colors, because dark mode needs a `.bp3-dark` selector:

```
"text-lg font-semibold leading-tight pb-2 border-0 border-b-2 border-solid dg-settings-heading"
```

Verified against Roam's actual stylesheet: 15.75px / 600, 2px solid rule in both themes, no stray top border. One deliberate change: the heading is 15.75px instead of 16px, since `text-lg` is the nearest step. Rows are 14px, so it still outranks them.

## 3. The `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` comment

[Michael's comment](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3985273833) on [CanvasShortcutSettings.tsx:106](apps/roam/src/components/settings/CanvasShortcutSettings.tsx:106) — he asked "Is `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` recognized in roam?"

Answer: **no.** Roam's Tailwind predates JIT, so it contains **zero** arbitrary-value rules. `grid-template-columns` computes to `none` — the "two-column" shortcut grid has been falling back to one implicit column since #952 shipped it. Not introduced here; the line only appears in the diff because the file moved.

It's not isolated — 9 call sites in apps/roam use arbitrary values and all are inert:

- `text-[#5c7080]`, `bg-[#f7f9fc]`, `border-[#d3d8de]`, `text-[13px]` (DiscourseNodeMenu, CanvasEmbedDialog, RelationTypeDropdown)
- `min-w-[160px]`, `max-h-[240px]` (PageGroupPanel, RelationTypeDropdown)
- `font-[inherit] text-[inherit]` (DiscourseRelationConfigPanel)

Worth its own ticket. Want me to draft one?

## 5. `resolveSettingsTabId` — Michael's premise is half right

He's right that we never pass an *unknown* id. He's wrong that the id is always known: **two entry points pass nothing at all**.

- [registerCommandPaletteCommands.ts:344](apps/roam/src/utils/registerCommandPaletteCommands.ts:344) — `renderSettings({ onloadArgs })`, the plain "open settings" command
- [DiscourseFloatingMenu.tsx:71](apps/roam/src/components/DiscourseFloatingMenu.tsx:71) — same

`selectedTabId` is optional on `SettingsDialog` precisely so those two can say "just open it". So `undefined` is a real, reachable case — and his suggested fix (default in the parameter) is the right shape for it, which is what I pushed.

The separate line-32 comment ("unknown ids pass through") is the weak one. Per-node tabs don't exist in this dialog — `DiscourseNodeConfigPanel` is nested *inside* the Nodes tab. Nothing passes a uid-keyed tab id. I'd delete that comment; the passthrough is just the `??` fallback, not a documented contract.

## 4. "Saved deep link" — he's right, the term is wrong

There is no URL-level deep link. Nothing anywhere parses a tab id out of a hash or query string. The only callers of `selectedTabId` are three in-repo ones, all already updated in this PR.

So nothing "saves" one. `SETTINGS_TAB_ALIASES` is defensive coverage for callers outside the repo — `SettingsDialog` is exported, and a user script or another extension could pass an old id. That's a much weaker justification than the comment implies. Two honest options: reword to say exactly that, or drop the alias map. I'd keep the map (it's 9 lines and protects against silent wrong-tab landings) and rewrite the comment. Your call.

## ENG-2173 — comment only, the code is fine

Nothing to fix behaviorally. ENG-2173 (`8a6d5379f`, on `main`) doesn't change the schema default — `zodSchema.ts` still says `.default(false)`. It added `migratePropsStoreDefault.ts`, which at startup writes `Use new settings store: true` into the graph's feature-flag block props. And `bulkReadSettings` still falls back to `readAllLegacyPersonalSettings()` for any user whose personal migration marker isn't set.

So the legacy config tree that `useLegacyConfigBlocks` writes to is still read, and the dual-write is still correct. What changed is only the *framing*: `false` is no longer what a real graph runs with. My comment asserted it was "the default", which is why he flagged it. Reworded, no code change needed.

Also worth knowing: **ENG-2173 is not in this stack's base.** `roam-setting-overhaul` branched before it, so it arrives at merge time. Nothing here conflicts with it.

## 1. Feature-gated tab hiding — the options

You said keep it. The constraint that forced it out is: *a tab that hides itself cannot host the control that un-hides it.* So the question is only where the "Enable left sidebar" toggle goes. Four shapes:

**A. Toggle back to Preferences → General; tab hidden when off.** Restores the pre-PR arrangement: `hidden={!leftSidebarEnabled}` on the tab, plus the `visibleTabId` guard that bounces the selection to a safe tab. Closest to the original scoping and to what Michael asked for. Cost: the toggle sits two tabs away from everything it controls, which is the wart the taxonomy was meant to remove. Also the command-palette entry that deep-links to the Left sidebar tab needs to handle the tab being hidden.

**B. Toggle to the Admin panel, with the other feature flags.** `Suggestive mode overlay`, `Advanced node search`, `Node sharing`, `Use new settings store` already live there. This is the cleanest answer to Michael's actual open question ("where should feature flags live") and it pre-answers the admin-gating he expects. Cost: a non-admin can't turn the left sidebar on at all any more — that may be exactly the intent, or a behavior change that needs its own decision.

**C. Toggle stays on the Left sidebar tab; tab hidden when off (current PR + hiding).** Internally contradictory — once you turn it off, you can't turn it back on. Not viable, listed only to rule it out.

**D. Tab always visible, but an empty state instead of blank.** "Left sidebar is disabled — enable it in Preferences → General." Fixes the blank-screen UX Michael flagged without hiding anything. Doesn't satisfy "keep the hiding", so it's a complement to A or B, not a substitute.

My read: **B, with D's empty state as a safety net if a deep link lands someone on a hidden tab.** It answers the flag-location question once rather than per-feature, and it matches where the admin gating is going anyway. But B changes who can enable the feature, so it's a product call — and Michael explicitly said he's unsure whether you two re-clarified the scoping. That's the one to settle with him directly.

---

CI is green on both pushes. I haven't replied on GitHub about the Tailwind findings or the deep-link wording yet — say the word and I'll post them.
what do you mean "Roam's Tailwind predates JIT,"?
Good question to push on — my phrasing conflated two things. Let me check the more important one.

Two different things were packed into that phrase, and only one of them is the real constraint. Let me separate them.

**What "predates JIT" means.** Arbitrary values — the `[...]` bracket syntax like `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` or `text-[13px]` — aren't a CSS feature, they're a *compiler* feature. Classic Tailwind generated a fixed catalog of utilities from your config ahead of time; a class had to be in that catalog or it didn't exist. There was no mechanism to invent `w-[762px]` on demand, because nothing was reading your markup at build time. The JIT engine changed that: it scans your source files and generates a rule for whatever it finds, including bracket syntax. JIT shipped as opt-in in Tailwind 2.1 and became the only engine in v3.

Roam's `tailwind.min.css` is a pre-generated v2-era file. I confirmed the era from what's in and out of it: `backdrop-blur-sm` is there (v2.x), `snap-center` and `break-inside-avoid` are not (both v3 additions). And the decisive check — **zero selectors in all 6550 rules contain a bracket**. So the brackets aren't failing to match; those rules were never generated.

**The correction worth making.** I implied our classes work by coincidence of Roam happening to use them. That's wrong, and I checked rather than leave it standing. I probed utilities no human writes by hand — `gap-72`, `skew-y-12`, `col-start-7`, `place-content-evenly`, `divide-y-reverse` — and every one is present. That's a **full, unpurged build**: the entire v2 default catalog, not a subset purged down to Roam's own markup.

That's a much better situation than "coincidence." The practical rule for apps/roam is:

- Any standard Tailwind 2 utility works — you're not limited to what Roam itself uses.
- Arbitrary `[...]` values never work. Use a CSS rule.
- v3-era utilities never work (scroll snap, `break-inside-*`, the v3 color additions).
- Preflight is separately absent, which is why `border-b-2` needs `border-0 border-solid` — that's an unrelated gap from the JIT question.
- `1rem` is 14px here, so `text-base` is 14px, not 16px.

I've saved this to memory so it doesn't need re-deriving. The reproduction is cheap if you ever want to confirm: open roamresearch.com, append an element with the classes, read `getComputedStyle`.
then is there a good reason why we're using abritrary values instead of a catalog one?
Worth checking rather than assuming. Let me see whether each site actually had a catalog option.

No. In every one of the nine cases the arbitrary class produces *nothing* — so whatever the motivation, the mechanism was never right. But the wants behind them split into three groups, and they're not equally defensible.

**Colors — six of the nine sites, and the least defensible.** `text-[#5c7080]`, `border-[#d3d8de]`, `hover:bg-[#f7f9fc]`, `bg-[#333]`, `hover:bg-[#f0f0f0]`. These are Blueprint palette hexes; `#5c7080` is Blueprint's gray1. The want is real — Tailwind's gray ramp doesn't contain them (`gray-500` is `#6b7280`, a different hue), so no catalog class hits those values. But apps/roam/AGENTS.md already says not to introduce arbitrary colors and to reach for Blueprint or Roam-native styling instead, which is the actual answer here. Worth noting: these elements are currently rendering with inherited defaults and nobody has filed a bug, which suggests the exact hexes weren't load-bearing to begin with.

**Genuine catalog gaps — two sites.** `min-w-[160px]`: Tailwind 2 ships only `min-w-0 / full / min / max`, no scale values, so there is no catalog class for this. `font-[inherit] text-[inherit]`: v2 has no `inherit` utilities at all. Both of these really do need a CSS rule — there was never a Tailwind way to write them in this build.

**Had a catalog option — the rest.** `max-h-[240px]` could be `max-h-60` (15rem, 210px at Roam's 14px root — not identical, but a scale value). `text-[13px]` is near `text-sm`. `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` is the interesting one: `grid-cols-2` exists but means two equal fractions, whereas `auto auto` means size-to-content. Different intent — and for a label/control pair, a flex row is the better fix anyway.

**Why it happened.** Bracket syntax is muscle memory from Tailwind 3, and nothing in this app pushes back. apps/roam has no Tailwind build — `tailwind.config.ts` is literally commented "required for editor support" with `content: []`. So there's no compiler to reject the class, no purge step, no lint rule. The string lands in the DOM and silently does nothing. Editor tooling makes it *worse*, since your IDE autocompletes against a Tailwind 3 config that doesn't describe what Roam serves.

That's the part worth fixing structurally rather than site by site: an ESLint rule banning bracket classes in apps/roam would catch this at review time and cost nothing ongoing — CI already surfaces new lint findings on changed lines. Want me to fold that into the ticket for the nine sites?
yes, then use flex row instead of this grid-cols and test it out

# DG Create Engineering Ticket

## Problem

- What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

## Done When

- Describe how success is verified (behavioral or technical).
- Remember: Make only the smallest change needed to solve the problem.
- Remember: **Stay within the defined scope, or communicate any scope increase**

## Out of Scope

- (Optional) What adjacent cases, abstractions, or future work are explicitly not included?
- Link follow-up tickets where applicable

## Notes

- Additional Context, Blockers, dependencies, or follow-up actions.
```

Every bullet above is placeholder guidance. Replace or remove every placeholder before presenting a draft or creating a ticket. Keep all five headings, leaving `Out of Scope` or `Notes` empty when nothing useful applies. Use 1–3 short bullets per section unless the ticket is genuinely complex.

## Ticket readiness

Always use the Engineering team. This skill never creates or redirects to Feedback.

- Use `Backlog` when the problem is known, the fix is agreed upon, and another engineer can implement it without further product or solution decisions.
- Use `Triage` when implementation is likely within six months but the decision, scope, or solution is not fully settled.
- Keep an explicit Engineering ticket request in Engineering even when it is idea-stage.

## Project selection

Every ticket must use an existing project that is not completed, canceled, archived, or trashed. Resolve the project in this order:

1. Use the project explicitly named by the user.
2. Use a clearly relevant active project from the current work context.
3. For Roam work, use `Roam Discourse Graph plugin assorted tasks`.
4. For Obsidian work, use `Obsidian Discourse Graphs plugin assorted tasks`.
5. Otherwise, use `Engineering Ops assorted tasks`.

Confirm the selected project still exists, is active, and includes the Engineering team. Never create a project. If a user-specified project is missing, ambiguous, or inactive, ask the user for another project instead of silently substituting one.

## Labels and optional fields

- Inspect existing issue labels and apply every clearly relevant label.
- Never create a label or guess an uncertain label.
- Missing or uncertain labels do not block creation. After creation, tell the user when no label was applied or when label selection remained uncertain.
- Set priority only when the user or context makes it clear and useful.
- Do not set a cycle or release. CI/CD handles releases.

## Create or draft

Draft without changing Linear when the user asks for a draft, review, or rewrite. Create the ticket without an additional confirmation when the user explicitly asks to create it.

Before creation, resolve the current Engineering statuses, selected project, and existing labels. Create the issue once with its title, completed description, status, project, labels, and justified priority. If the result is ambiguous, search for the issue before retrying so a transient failure does not create a duplicate.

After creation, return the issue identifier, title, status, project, and link. Include the generated branch name when Linear returns one. Do not restate the full description unless the user asks.

input.description:
## Problem

- apps/roam builds no CSS of its own. Its Tailwind classes resolve against Roam's prebuilt `assets/css/tailwind.min.css`, a pre-JIT Tailwind 2 build whose ~6550 rules contain **zero** bracket selectors. Every arbitrary-value class (`text-[13px]`, `min-w-[160px]`, `bg-[#333]`) is therefore inert — the property is simply never applied.
- Nine such call sites exist today. Nothing pushes back on them: `tailwind.config.ts` has `content: []` and is documented as existing only for editor support, so there is no compiler, no purge step, and no lint rule. Editor autocomplete makes it worse by suggesting Tailwind 3 syntax that this build does not contain.
- No user-visible regression is known — the properties never applied and nobody has reported it. The cost is silent dead styling that keeps accruing.

## Solution

- Replace each arbitrary-value class with a catalog utility where one exists. The build is full and unpurged, so every standard Tailwind 2 utility is available.
- For the genuine v2 gaps — `min-w` at a px value, and `font-[inherit]` / `text-[inherit]`, neither of which v2 has utilities for — use a CSS rule instead.
- The hex colors are Blueprint palette values. `apps/roam/AGENTS.md` already says to prefer Blueprint and Roam-native styling over arbitrary colors, so use Blueprint classes rather than reproducing the hex.
- Add an ESLint rule banning bracket classes in apps/roam so this cannot regress.

### Call sites

| File | Classes |
| --- | --- |
| `components/DiscourseNodeMenu.tsx:382` | `border-[#d3d8de]`, `hover:border-[#bfccd6]`, `hover:bg-[#f7f9fc]` |
| `components/settings/DiscourseRelationConfigPanel.tsx:1130` | `font-[inherit]`, `text-[inherit]` |
| `components/settings/PageGroupPanel.tsx:184` | `min-w-[160px]` |
| `components/canvas/CanvasEmbedDialog.tsx:37`, `:41` | `text-[#5c7080]` |
| `components/canvas/overlays/RelationTypeDropdown.tsx:84` | `max-h-[240px]`, `min-w-[160px]` |
| `components/canvas/overlays/RelationTypeDropdown.tsx:92` | `text-[13px]`, `text-[#333]`, `hover:bg-[#f0f0f0]` |
| `components/canvas/overlays/RelationTypeDropdown.tsx:106` | `bg-[#333]` |

## Done When

- No bracket-syntax Tailwind class remains in `apps/roam/src`.
- Each affected element renders with the intended styling, confirmed against Roam's own stylesheet.
- The ESLint rule fails on a newly introduced bracket class in apps/roam. CI already reports new lint findings on changed lines, so no workflow change is needed.

## Out of Scope

- Building a real Tailwind pipeline for apps/roam.
- The two adjacent constraints of the same build, which are correct in the code today and only need to stay that way: preflight is absent, so a bare `border-b-2` paints nothing and needs `border-0 border-b-2 border-solid`; and the root font-size is 14px, so `text-base` is 14px rather than 16px.

## Notes

- Verified by loading roamresearch.com, appending elements with the classes, and reading `getComputedStyle` — the same check reproduces any of this in a minute.
- Tailwind 3-era utilities (`snap-*`, `break-inside-*`) are absent for the same reason and should be treated the same way.
- A tenth site, `grid-cols-[auto_auto]` in `CanvasShortcutSettings.tsx`, was removed in [PR 1373](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373). That layout was never broken — `col-span-2` on the header was creating the implicit second column — which is a good illustration of why these are hard to spot.

content.text:
All green. Here's the answer to your question about the tab selection.

## What the two variables actually were

The old code kept **two** pieces of state that were normally identical:

```
activeTabId   // what the user selected — the source of truth
visibleTabId  // what gets displayed — activeTabId, unless it points at a hidden tab
```

`visibleTabId` diverged from `activeTabId` in exactly one case: the selection was one of the two left-sidebar tabs *and* the feature was off. In that case it substituted `homePersonal`.

## Why that substitution was doing real work

I checked Blueprint's source rather than assume, and it's worse than I'd have guessed: **`hidden` is not a Blueprint prop at all.** It falls through `htmlProps` onto the tab title `<div>` as the native HTML `hidden` attribute. Blueprint has no concept of a hidden tab.

Which means the panel rendering ignores it completely. With `renderActiveTabPanelOnly={true}` — which [Settings.tsx:174](apps/roam/src/components/settings/Settings.tsx:174) sets — Blueprint filters panels by `tab.props.id === selectedTabId` and nothing else. So if `selectedTabId` points at a hidden tab you get a broken dialog: the left sidebar panel renders in the body while no tab button is highlighted in the list, because the button it corresponds to is `hidden`. The user sees settings they can't navigate back to.

`visibleTabId` was the thing preventing that. Not decoration.

There's a second, subtler property worth noticing: because it redirected *display* and left `activeTabId` alone, the original target survived. Enable the left sidebar with the dialog still open → `leftSidebarEnabled` flips → the substitution stops applying → the user snaps to the left-sidebar tab they were originally deep-linked to. Resetting `activeTabId` instead would have thrown that away.

## What my change means

Given the current PR's design, nothing. One Left sidebar tab, never hidden, so `visibleTabId` could not differ from `activeTabId` — the guard had no reachable case and deleting it was a genuine no-op.

But that's the point: **the deletion was only valid as a consequence of the design decision Michael is pushing back on.** It wasn't an independent cleanup. The moment you restore feature-gated hiding — which you've said you want — the guard has a live case again and has to come back, because the deep link from the command palette and from [LeftSidebarView.tsx:868](apps/roam/src/components/LeftSidebarView.tsx:868) can still target that tab while the feature is off.

So the two review threads are one decision, not two. Whatever you settle with Michael on where the flag lives, restoring the hiding brings the guard back with it — and if the toggle moves to Admin or Preferences, the guard's fallback should point at *that* tab, not General, so a deep link lands somewhere the user can actually act.

I'd rather not write that code until you've settled the flag's location with him, since the fallback target depends on the answer.

## Also done this turn

- **ENG-2096 cleanup** — you were right, and the consequence was concrete. Main has zero references to the canvas overlay left; our branch still carries the key, schema, accessor mapping, and consumer. Because this PR *re-homes* the panel into `DiscourseContextSettings.tsx`, a file that doesn't exist on main, git would have kept our copy while main's side deleted the key it references — a type error surfacing only at merge. Panel and its import removed; I left the key/schema/consumer alone so main's deletions apply cleanly. Typecheck and 142 tests pass.
- **`grid-cols-[auto_auto]` → flex rows**, and a correction: I told you the grid was rendering as a single column. **That was wrong.** `col-span-2` on the header forces an implicit second column, and implicit columns are auto-sized — which is exactly what `auto auto` would have done. All green (each check shows pending then pass across the two pushes).

## The comment you meant

It was a CodeRabbit **nitpick inside a review body**, not an inline thread — which is why it never appeared in my thread sweep. GitHub's `reviewThreads` query only returns inline threads; findings in the review summary itself live in a different place. Worth knowing for future sweeps.

It flagged six components missing explicit return types, `LeftSidebarSettings.tsx:12` among them, against AGENTS.md's "Use explicit return types for functions." Valid — all six are components this PR created or moved. Added `: React.ReactElement` to `SettingsSectionHeading`, `SettingsGroup`, `SettingTitle`, `PreferencesGeneral`, `CanvasSettings`, and `LeftSidebarSettings`. Typecheck, 142 tests, lint clean; pushed.

One other thing in that sweep you may not have registered: Graphite posted a **PR size warning** — over the ~200-line guideline, and it asks for either a split or a written justification in the PR body. Nothing has been added. That's a merge-time nag worth settling.

## Consequences of going back to `visibleTabId`

**It stays coherent, because it lies to Blueprint on purpose.** Passing `visibleTabId` as `selectedTabId` means Blueprint's internal state *is* the fallback tab — so General's title highlights, General's panel renders, and the dialog looks entirely normal. The user never sees a half-state. That's the whole reason it works.

**The divergence is contained but not zero.** `activeTabId` keeps holding the hidden id. Two places feel that:

- The settings snapshot is memoised on it — `useMemo(() => bulkReadSettings(), [activeTabId])`. Harmless here: any later tab click updates `activeTabId` and re-triggers the read.
- The snap-back. If the feature gets enabled while the dialog is open, `leftSidebarTabHidden` flips false, `visibleTabId` falls through to `activeTabId`, and the user is suddenly moved to the Left sidebar tab. Read generously that's the deep link finally being honoured; read plainly it's an unrequested jump. Worth deciding which you want rather than inheriting it.

**Without the guard, restoring hiding is actively broken.** I checked Blueprint's source: `hidden` isn't a Blueprint prop at all, it falls through to the tab title `<div>` as the native HTML attribute. Blueprint has no concept of a hidden tab, and with `renderActiveTabPanelOnly` it filters panels purely on `id === selectedTabId`. So a deep link to a hidden tab renders that panel while its title is `hidden` — nothing in the list is highlighted, and the user is looking at settings with no way back. The guard is the only thing standing between you and that. Keep hiding ⇒ keep the guard, not optional.

**The part that couples to your flag decision.** The fallback target isn't arbitrary — it's the answer to "where do we send someone whose deep link is unreachable?" The old code sent them to `homePersonal`, which was exactly where the enable toggle lived. That's coherent: you land on the tab holding the switch for the thing you were trying to reach. If the flag moves to Admin and the fallback still says Preferences → General, you've landed the user somewhere with no way to enable what they asked for. So:

- Flag → Preferences → General ⇒ fallback is General. One-line restore of the old code.
- Flag → Admin panel ⇒ fallback should be the Admin tab, which is itself conditionally shown (`showAdminPanel`), so the guard needs a second condition — and a non-admin has no reachable destination at all, which pushes you toward the empty-state option instead of a redirect.

That second branch is why I'd still rather not write it until you've settled the location with Michael: it's not the same change in both worlds, and the Admin variant needs a real answer for non-admins.
what's some popular pattern for disabling a setting -> it doesn't show up in the navigation anymore? is it anti-pattern? what are the popular apps like notion or linear doing about this?
Let me verify one concrete example rather than rely on recall.

Checked Linear's own docs rather than recall, and the answer is directly relevant.

## The distinction that actually decides this

The question isn't "hide or show." It's **what kind of gate is this?** Three kinds, three different conventions:

**1. Entitlement gates** — your plan doesn't include it. Almost universally *shown*, often with a lock or upgrade prompt. Hiding destroys the upsell, and "where is that feature I read about" is a worse experience than "you need to upgrade."

**2. Permission gates** — you're not an admin. Usually *hidden*. There's no action the user could take, so the entry is pure clutter. Notion is the example I'd point at: workspace settings sections are role-scoped, and a member simply doesn't see admin-only sections. (Stated from knowledge — I didn't verify it just now, and these UIs change.)

**3. Preference toggles** — someone turned it off. The section *stays*, because settings is where you go to change settings. Hiding the way back is the failure mode.

## What Linear does — verified

From [Linear's cycles docs](https://linear.app/docs/use-cycles):

> "Configure cycles under **Team Settings > Cycles**. Turn on the toggle for **Enable cycles**."

and, on disabling:

> "You can choose to reenable cycles at any stage in the future."

So for a feature-sized toggle, Linear puts the enable switch **on the feature's own settings page**, and that page stays reachable when the feature is off. That is exactly the shape this PR currently has.

The split worth naming for Michael: Linear hides Cycles from the **product** navigation when off — no Cycles entry in the sidebar — while keeping it in **settings** navigation. Those are two different navigations with opposite rules. Hiding a feature's UI when disabled is correct. Hiding its *settings* is the part that bites.

## Is hiding an anti-pattern?

Hiding a settings entry isn't inherently one — case 2 above is legitimate and common. But one specific version of it is, unambiguously: **hiding the only control that can reverse the state.** A trap door. Turn the toggle off, the tab vanishes, and the switch you need is inside the thing that vanished. That's the objection I raised in the original PR comment, and it holds regardless of which philosophy you prefer.

Which is why the mainstream solution isn't "hide vs. show" at all — it's **progressive disclosure**: the enable toggle sits at the top of the section, and the dependent settings appear beneath it only when on. iOS Settings does this constantly. It's what this PR does today, and it's what Linear does.

## How this lands on your decision

Michael's two objections split cleanly under that framing, and they don't both survive:

- *"We lose hiding the Left Sidebar tab when disabled"* — this treats the flag as a preference toggle, where the convention runs the other way. Linear is a direct counterexample.
- *"Poor UX for non-admins who see a blank screen, since the toggle should/will be admin-gated"* — this is the strong one, and it's a **different case**. If non-admins can't flip it, the tab is case 2, and hiding it from them is conventional and right.

So both of you are right about different users. The pattern that satisfies both is role-dependent, not flag-dependent:

- **Admins**: tab always visible, toggle at top, sections disclosed beneath. Linear's shape, and no trap door.
- **Non-admins**: tab hidden — not because the feature is off, but because they have no control to exercise. Same rule Notion applies to admin-only sections.

That also dissolves the `visibleTabId` problem in the admin case (nothing to redirect, since the tab never hides for them) while keeping the guard for the non-admin case, where a deep link genuinely can point somewhere unreachable.

Worth noting this depends on admin-gating that doesn't exist yet — Michael said "should/will be." So the honest sequencing question for him is whether to build the role-conditional version now or ship the always-visible tab and revisit when the gating lands.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

content.text:
Checked, and the answer is no, and the reason is the interesting part.

**The block text isn't in our code. It's data in the user's graph.** Those strings are child blocks on the `[[discourse graph/config]]` page in every user's Roam graph. `trigger`, `Canvas Page Format`, `(BETA) Left Sidebar` are the block text itself, and it's the lookup key: `getUidAndStringSetting({ tree, text: "trigger" })` walks the tree matching that string exactly.

So renaming isn't an edit, it's a **data migration on every existing graph**. And the readers are spread out, three or four per setting:

- `trigger` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:67`, `accessors.ts:396`, `init.ts:88`
- `(BETA) Left Sidebar` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:79`, `accessors.ts:720`, `registerCommandPaletteCommands.ts:452`
- `Canvas Page Format` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:72`, `accessors.ts:403`

Updating those is mechanical. The migration isn't. Any graph that doesn't get migrated has a block named `trigger` while the code looks for `Graph-wide default`, finds nothing, and falls back to the default. The user's trigger silently resets. That's the failure mode this PR is specifically trying not to cause, and it's the same one I flagged on the settings-search addressing.

There's also a user-visible angle: `[[discourse graph/config]]` is a real page they can open. Renaming its blocks changes something they may have linked or referenced.

**And the store is on its way out.** ENG-2173 turned props-based settings on by default, so this tree is now a fallback for un-migrated users. Paying for a rename migration on a store you're retiring, at the risk of orphaning settings, to fix a cosmetic mismatch nobody sees, is a bad trade.

The deeper point worth making to Michael: the mismatch exists because the legacy store used **human-readable UI labels as storage keys**. That's the original design mistake. The props store fixed it with stable keys in `settingKeys.ts` that don't move when labels change. `blockKey` is just the adapter between the two eras, and it's the standard display-name-vs-persisted-key split.

So keeping `blockKey` is the cheap direction: UI labels stay free to change (this PR renames one), and the storage key stays pinned. Renaming the blocks would re-couple them, on the store we're abandoning.

That's probably a better reply to him than the one I drafted, since it answers the question he'd ask next. Want me to fold it in and post?

Yes for `blockKey` specifically — but not for the mechanism it belongs to, and the distinction matters.

**`blockKey` is legacy-only.** The only places it's ever supplied are the three `{...legacyBlocks.*}` spreads in `PreferencesGeneral`, `CanvasSettings`, and `LeftSidebarSettings`. The one other occurrence, `blockKey={blockKey}` at `BlockPropSettingPanels.tsx:575`, is an internal pass-through between panel components, not a call site.

**The block-sync props it sits alongside are not.** `parentUid`, `uid`, and `order` are used widely and currently: `DiscourseNodeSpecification`, `DiscourseNodeSuggestiveRules`, `ExportSettings`, and others. Those panels also write to Roam blocks. They just never need `blockKey`, because their visible title already equals the block text.

Which is exactly the point, and it's visible in the code. Look at `ExportSettings.tsx:25`:

```tsx
{/* TODO: Titles kept as lowercase to match legacy readers in getExportSettings.ts.
    Update titles to Sentence case once read side is migrated to block props. */}
<GlobalFlagPanel title="remove special characters" ...
```

That panel has a lowercase, ungrammatical UI label, deliberately, because the label doubles as the storage key and the readers match it. They took the other branch of the same fork: instead of decoupling with `blockKey`, they froze the UI label to protect the storage.

So `blockKey` isn't a legacy wart, it's the escape hatch from that constraint. Three settings in this PR needed a better label than their block text allowed, and got one. `ExportSettings` still has a `TODO` waiting for the same freedom.

That reframes the answer to Michael. The honest version isn't "this is legacy cruft we tolerate", it's: **wherever a panel writes to a Roam block, the block text is the storage key, so the UI label is pinned to it unless you decouple them. `blockKey` is that decoupling.** It applies to legacy config-page settings today because those are the ones whose labels this PR changed, and it's the mechanism `ExportSettings` would use to clear its TODO.

Which also answers your earlier question from the other direction: renaming the blocks would re-pin label to storage for all of them, and re-introduce the constraint that TODO is complaining about.

Done — and it turned out better than "closest Tailwind color."

## `settingsStyles.css` no longer has any of it

The file is back to just `.bp3-tab-copy`. The whole `.dg-settings-heading` rule and the `.bp3-dark` override are gone.

```
"bp3-heading mb-0 text-lg leading-tight pb-2 border-0 border-b-2 border-solid border-gray-300"
```

## Why not a Tailwind color for the text

I measured the nearest matches against Roam's actual sheet. For `#182026` it's `text-gray-900` at distance 10.7; for `#f5f8fa` it's `text-gray-100` at 6. Close enough to use — except **there's no way to switch between them.** I checked: Roam's Tailwind build contains **zero `dark:` variant rules** (the only "dark" selectors in it are `mix-blend-darken` and friends). And even if it had them, Tailwind's class strategy keys on `.dark` while Roam themes on `.bp3-dark`. So a Tailwind color would have pinned one value across both themes — near-black text on a dark background.

**`.bp3-heading` solves it outright.** Measured inside a real `.bp3-dialog`:

| | light | dark |
|---|---|---|
| `.bp3-heading` | `rgb(24,32,38)` | `rgb(245,248,250)` |
| what I'd hardcoded | `#182026` | `#f5f8fa` |

Identical, both themes, and `font-weight: 600` included — so `font-semibold` came out too. My CSS was hand-reimplementing a Blueprint class that already existed, which is also the thing `apps/roam/AGENTS.md` puts first in its priority order. One addition needed: `bp3-heading` carries `margin-bottom: 10px`, so `mb-0` cancels it and the group's `gap-1` stays in charge.

The border does use Tailwind: `border-gray-300` (`rgb(209,213,219)`), the nearest catalog value to the old `rgba(16,22,26,0.15)`. **Caveat worth your call:** unlike the text it doesn't theme, so in dark mode it's a light rule on a dark ground rather than Blueprint's own convention (dark dividers go *darker*, `rgba(16,22,26,0.4)`). It's visible and legible either way, just brighter than Blueprint would draw it. If you'd rather it match convention, that needs one `.bp3-dark` rule back — your call, since the whole point was emptying that file.

## What I verified, and what I didn't

Verified against the real `blueprint.css` and `tailwind.min.css` that Roam serves, with computed styles on real `.bp3-dialog` markup in both themes. That's what determines the colors, so the color question is settled.

content.text:
You were right, and the fix is much simpler than what I did.

## What I got wrong

I hand-retyped ENG-2096's deletions onto branches whose base doesn't have them. That invented a second, divergent copy of a change that already exists on `main`, and dragged `DiscourseNodeUtil.tsx`, `userSettings.ts`, `zodSchema.ts` and `accessors.ts` into a PR that has no business touching them. Both commits are dropped and force-pushed away:

- PR 1373 is back at `b4c65faea`, with no canvas or key-file changes in its diff
- PR 1379 is back at `03d0bf060`, typecheck clean

The one overlay change I'm leaving in place is the panel row in `DiscourseContextSettings.tsx`, because that file is **new in this PR** — `main`'s deletion can't reach a file `main` doesn't have, so it's genuinely ours to not re-add.

## Why the base is stale, and how little it takes to fix

`roam-setting-overhaul` is **47 commits behind `main` and 0 ahead.** It has no commits of its own and no PR of its own — it's just a stale pointer into `main`'s history. Git confirms it's a pure fast-forward ancestor.

So it doesn't need a rebase. It needs a **fast-forward**:

```bash
git push origin origin/main:roam-setting-overhaul
```

Nothing is rewritten, nothing is lost, no conflicts are possible at that step. And it brings in ENG-2096 *and* ENG-2173 (the props-default flip, the thing behind Michael's stale-comment note), so both of those stop being things the stack has to work around.

## What it costs downstream — your call before I push

Every stacked PR is yours, which keeps this contained:

```
roam-setting-overhaul (→ main)
 └─ #1373 eng-2189
     └─ #1375 eng-2186
         ├─ #1420 eng-2188
         └─ #1424 eng-2185   ← duplicate head, see below
             └─ #1374 eng-2185
                 └─ #1421 eng-2183
                     └─ #1379 eng-2213
                         └─ #1378 eng-2184
```

After the fast-forward, each branch needs `main` merged through it in order, and *that* is where conflicts will surface — the overlay removal will land as a real conflict wherever a branch moved the code that `main` deleted. Which is the correct place to resolve it, instead of me pre-empting it by hand.

Two things worth deciding first:

1. **`eng-2185` has two open PRs** — #1424 based on `eng-2186`, #1374 based on `eng-2188` — same head branch, different bases. One of them is wrong, and the stack order can't be resolved until you say which.
2. **Fast-forward now or after 1373 merges?** Doing it now means seven PRs go out-of-date and re-run CI at once, while 1373 is still under review from Michael. Doing it after 1373 merges is quieter but leaves 1373's diff sitting on a 47-commit-stale base a while longer.

Tell me which, and whether #1424 or #1374 is the keeper, and I'll run the fast-forward and cascade the merges in order.
PR1374 is the correct one. i closed the PR 1424. we should fast forward the base then rebase everything on top of the stack

Done. The whole stack now sits on `main`.

## What changed

`roam-setting-overhaul` was fast-forwarded to `main` (it had 0 unique commits, so nothing was rewritten), then all seven branches were rebased in order and force-pushed. Every one typechecks and passes tests; PR 1373 is green and `MERGEABLE/CLEAN`.

```

All bases verified correct after closing 1424. Pre-rebase SHAs are saved at `scratchpad/stack-recovery.txt` if anything needs backing out.

## Your point, confirmed by the result

PR 1373 no longer touches `DiscourseNodeUtil.tsx`, `userSettings.ts`, `settingKeys.ts` or `zodSchema.ts` at all — the overlay removal now arrives from `main`, where it belongs. And the one place the stack genuinely had to act showed up on its own: after the rebase, 2213 failed to compile with

```
'"PERSONAL_KEYS.overlayInCanvas"' does not exist in type 'Record<RowKeyId, AuthoredSetting>'
```

That's the exhaustive catalog doing its job. One line deleted in `settingsCatalog.ts` — the only hand-written change the removal actually required, in the only branch that owns it. Which is the version of this I should have arrived at instead of retyping main's deletions across two branches.

## Conflict resolutions worth reviewing

Most were mechanical, but these involved judgment:

- **PreferencesGeneral (2189)** — `main` still had the rows this PR relocated. I verified each one survives elsewhere before dropping main's copies: Text selection popup and Disable sidebar open stay in the file, Hide feedback button and Streamline styling went to PreferencesStyling, Auto canvas relations to CanvasSettings.
- **settingsTabs (2186, 2213)** — combined rather than picked: 2186's `SettingsTabId`/`isSettingsTabId`, 2213's `SETTINGS_TAB_META`, and 2189's default-parameter `resolveSettingsTabId` plus the reworded alias comment all survive.
- **PreferencesGeneral (2183)** — took 2183's `SettingItemRow` rewrite but dropped the `placeholder=""` it reintroduced, preserving the codex fix.
- **Dead CSS vars** — `--dg-secondary` is now unused (the header dot became Tailwind on 2186), so I dropped it; `--dg-primary` is kept because 2184's search field uses it. Worth a glance since the neutral vars remain defined on 2183+ where the row styles consume them.

## Still open

- The four downstream PRs show `UNSTABLE` — their CI is running or has non-blocking failures. Want me to watch and fix those too?
- Michael's feature-flag decision on the Left sidebar tab is still the one thing blocking 1373 on substance, and the `visibleTabId` guard comes back with whatever you two decide.
- The Graphite PR-size warning on 1373 still has no justification comment.
- `~/roam-ext-dev` points at this worktree but its build predates the rebase — say the word and I'll rebuild before any in-app check.

content.text:
Done and green.

## What changed

**`PreferencesGeneral.tsx`** — the `Enable left sidebar` toggle now lives here, at the bottom of the tab after the Node trigger group. Its reload prompt (`Alert`) and the PostHog capture moved with it, since both belong to the act of flipping the flag. The component takes `featureFlags` as a new prop, and carries the `legacyBlocks.leftSidebarFlag` spread so the legacy config block keeps being written by whichever panel owns the row.

**`LeftSidebarSettings.tsx`** — dropped to just its two sections. The `enabled` and `featureFlags` props, the `{enabled && …}` gate, the `Alert`, its `useState`, and the `useLegacyConfigBlocks` call are all gone; the component is now a plain arrow with no state at all.

**`Settings.tsx`** — `hidden={!leftSidebarEnabled}` back on the Left sidebar tab, and `selectedTabId` back to a computed `visibleTabId` that redirects to Preferences → General when the selection is left pointing at the hidden tab.

## Verified, not assumed

I built a throwaway SSR harness against the real Blueprint `Tabs` and deleted it after (nothing committed but the three source files). Three cases:

| case | tab hidden | panel shown |
|---|---|---|
| enabled, on sidebar tab | false | SIDEBAR |
| **disabled, no guard** | true | **SIDEBAR** |
| disabled, with guard | true | GENERAL |

The middle row is the one that matters: Blueprint hides the tab *title* but keeps rendering its panel, so without the redirect a deep link would show left-sidebar settings with nothing selected in the list. That's the concrete justification for restoring `visibleTabId` — it isn't ceremony.

Worth flagging one correction from earlier in this session: my first check reported the `hidden` attribute as absent. That was my regex, not Blueprint — the attribute renders before `data-tab-id`, so a pattern anchored after it never matched. The behaviour is as I originally described.

Typecheck, 383 tests, and lint all clean (the 4 remaining warnings are pre-existing enum-naming ones, untouched lines). CI on 1373 is fully green.

## Two things left

The downstream branches still pass the old props — they inherit this once each is merged forward, but 2186 onward will conflict in `Settings.tsx` around the tab block when you cascade. Happy to run that now, or leave it until 1373 lands.

And I haven't replied on Michael's two threads ([Settings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3985358088) and [LeftSidebarSettings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3985346115)) — those are the ones you wanted to handle yourself. If you'd like, I can post that the tab is feature-gated again with the toggle in General, and note that admin gating is deliberately left to its own ticket, which is the one part of his comment this doesn't cover.
cascade the rebase to the rest of the stack

Verified both code-changing findings — and #6 is real. Here's the triage.

## One actual bug, worth fixing before merge

**The legacy config tree is no longer refreshed before reading block uids.** The deleted `GeneralSettings` did this:

```ts
const settings = useMemo(() => {
  refreshConfigTree();                 // ← dropped
  const tree = discourseConfigRef.tree;
```

The new `useLegacyConfigBlocks` hook skips the refresh, with a comment claiming every writer and the dialog's close already cover it. That misses the first open, and any edit made directly on the `[[discourse graph/config]]` page. If the tree is stale, the hook gets `uid: undefined` for a block that exists, and the panel creates a **second** `trigger` / `Canvas Page Format` / `(BETA) Left Sidebar` block. Duplicate legacy blocks mean readers pick one arbitrarily. That's precisely the class of silent-reset bug this PR is careful about everywhere else. Fix is restoring one line.

## Small mandatory fixes

- `DiscourseContextSettings.tsx` and `PreferencesStyling.tsx` still lack explicit return types — CodeRabbit's list named six components, and these two weren't on it.
- My comment in `settingsTabs.ts` says "every in-repo call site is updated". That's PR history, not a lasting constraint, so it fails the style guide's durable-comment rule.

## One that conflicts with your own preference — your call

The check flags **no unit tests for `resolveSettingsTabId` and the alias map** as mandatory, and it's a fair target: pure functions, and your own inline annotation says a wrong alias fails silently. But your saved preference is throwaway harnesses, not committed tests, and the stack has commits literally titled "Drop unit tests." I won't override that on a checklist's say-so.

## PR body — needs your OK to edit

- **Mandatory:** the ~1,000-line diff needs a split justification, review entry points, and a testing path in the Reviewer brief. The body also predates main's template: no `## Standards check`, the Loom isn't under its heading, and Verification sits inside a `<details>` so it doesn't render as a heading.
- **Now false:** the *Left sidebar placement* bullet (it says the toggle stays on the tab), the *New behaviour* placeholder bullet (reverted), "the enable toggle gates the left sidebar sections", and "142/142 tests" (it's 383).
- Two of your inline self-annotations are stale too — [GeneralSettings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3895785239) names the wrong destination file and the wrong hook filename.

## What I couldn't verify

- **Scope vs. Done When** — Linear needs re-authorizing (`claude mcp` or your claude.ai connector settings), so the scope conclusion is blocked.
- **Roam manual testing** in the body predates the tab-hiding commit. Your new Loom may cover it; I can't watch videos.
